readerTitle: Why a longer wait can leave a better memory
caseNote: 실제 연구 (Kahneman 외 1993 찬물 실험, Redelmeier 외 2003 대장내시경 시험) + 가상 적용 (레스토랑, 구독형 앱)
insight: 고객은 경험 전체의 평균이 아니라 가장 강렬한 순간과 마지막 순간으로 기억한다. 그래서 개선 순서는 '마지막'부터다.
misconception: 경험은 짧을수록, 모든 단계가 고르게 좋을수록 좋게 기억된다.

sources.text: Kahneman, D., Fredrickson, B. L., Schreiber, C. A., & Redelmeier, D. A. (1993). When more pain is preferred to less: Adding a better end. Psychological Science, 4(6), 401–405.
Redelmeier, D. A., & Kahneman, D. (1996). Patients' memories of painful medical treatments. Pain, 66(1), 3–8.
Redelmeier, D. A., Katz, J., & Kahneman, D. (2003). Memories of colonoscopy: a randomized trial. Pain, 104(1–2), 187–194.
레스토랑과 앱 사례, 차트 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 찬물 실험 조건(약 14°C에서 60초, 긴 시행은 이어서 30초 동안 약 1°C 상승)과 '대부분이 긴 시행을 다시 하겠다고 선택' 결과를 1993년 원문으로 확인하세요. 비율(약 69%로 알려짐)은 확인 전이라 카드에 숫자를 쓰지 않았습니다.
2003년 대장내시경 무작위 시험: 시술 끝에 내시경을 잠시 더 두어 덜 불편한 구간을 추가했고, 환자들이 시술을 덜 불쾌하게 기억했으며 재검사 복귀가 다소 높았다는 내용을 원문으로 확인하세요. 표본 수와 효과 크기는 카드에 넣지 않았습니다.
차트의 순간별 점수(10점 만점)는 모두 가상 수치입니다. 평균 (8+9+7+3)÷4 = 6.75, 기억 점수는 정점 9와 끝 3의 평균 = 6으로 설명했습니다.
피크엔드 규칙은 실험실 연구에서 반복 확인되었지만 효과 크기는 상황에 따라 다르고, 기간을 완전히 무시하는 것은 아니라는 후속 연구가 있습니다. Watch out 카드 문구가 과장되지 않았는지 검토하세요.

cards.title: Why a longer wait can leave a better memory
body: In a 1993 study, people held a hand in painfully cold water twice. Once for 60 seconds. Once for 90 seconds, where the last 30 were slightly less cold.
Asked which one to repeat, most picked the longer one. More pain, chosen on purpose.

image.label: Two buckets of icy water with timers
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 얼음물 양동이 두 개와 타이머. 왼쪽 "60 sec", 오른쪽 "90 sec". 오른쪽 양동이 위에 작은 미소 표시와 따뜻해지는 색 그라데이션. 실제 브랜드나 로고 없음.

cards.title: One fix for your restaurant.
body: Guests rave about your food, but online ratings are stuck at average. You can afford one change this month.
Reviews mention three things: mains sometimes take a while, the dining room feels dated, and getting the bill at the end can take 15 minutes. Which do you fix?

options.text: Speed up the kitchen so mains arrive faster
options.feedback: Faster mains help, but they sit in the middle of a meal guests already enjoy. You spend effort where the memory is already good.

options.text: Fix the slow bill so the evening ends smoothly
options.feedback: The cheapest fix and the one guests will carry home. A sour last 15 minutes can color a great two hours.
It touches every minute of the visit, yet it's costly and changes little about how the evening feels when guests walk out.

cards.title: The longer trial wasn't better. It ended better.
body: In the cold-water study, the 90-second trial contained everything the 60-second one did, plus 30 more seconds of discomfort. By any total, it was worse.
But people didn't judge the total. They judged how it felt at its worst and how it felt when it stopped. The longer trial finished on a gentler note, so it was *remembered* as milder.
How long it lasted barely seemed to count.

cards.title: The peak-end rule
body: The **peak-end rule**: people judge a past experience mostly by its most intense moment and by how it ended, not by the average of every moment.
Its partner is **duration neglect**: the length of an experience matters much less to the memory than we expect.
That memory is what people use when deciding whether to come back or recommend you.

image.label: A wavy experience line with peak and end circled
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 시간에 따라 오르내리는 경험 곡선. 가장 높은 지점에 "Peak", 마지막 지점에 "End" 동그라미. 나머지 구간은 흐리게 처리하고 아래에 "What people remember" 라벨.

cards.title: It holds outside the lab, too.
body: Researchers Donald Redelmeier and Daniel Kahneman studied colonoscopy patients, a procedure many people dread. Patients' later ratings tracked the worst moment and the final minutes, not how long the procedure took.

In a 2003 randomized trial, doctors added a short, less uncomfortable stretch at the end for some patients. Those patients remembered the procedure as less unpleasant, and were somewhat more likely to return for later checks.
Same procedure, a little longer, better memory.

cards.title: A great meal, remembered as average.
body: Score each moment out of 10. The average is 6.75. But the memory leans on the peak (9) and the end (3), landing near 6.

groups.label: Guest's evening, moment by moment (out of 10)

cards.callout: Lift the ending to 8 and the memory rises more than any mid-meal fix could.
cards.softwareNote: In an app, the end is often a confirmation screen, a support chat closing, or a cancellation page. These moments get little design time but shape what users remember.

cards.title: A nice ending can't rescue a bad core.
body: The rule shapes memory, not reality. If the food is poor, a free mint at the door won't save you. And a painful peak still counts: one rude moment can define the whole visit.
For ongoing relationships, like a gym or a subscription, there are many small endings, not one. Each visit or session leaves its own memory.
Finally, engineering endings to hide real problems is manipulation. Customers notice, and trust breaks.

cards.title: Now it's a subscription app.
body: You run a budgeting app. Some users cancel every month. Today, cancelling takes five screens of warnings and a final page that says only "Your account has been closed."
Which cancellation flow best fits the peak-end rule?

options.text: Add more screens and a last-chance discount to keep people from leaving
options.feedback: You may save a few users, but everyone else leaves on a frustrating final memory, the one they'll share when friends ask about you.

options.text: Make cancelling quick, then end with a summary of what they saved and an easy way back
options.feedback: You give up a few forced saves and gain a warm last impression. Former users who leave well are more likely to return or recommend you.

options.text: Keep the flow, but rewrite the final page to sound friendlier
options.feedback: A kinder end helps, but five screens of warnings may become the peak users remember most.

cards.title: People remember the best moment and the last one.
body: Before spending on the whole experience, find its ending and its sharpest moment. Those two shape what customers remember and repeat.
**Try it today:** write down the last thing a customer sees, hears or does with your business. Is it something you designed, or something left over?

image.label: A door closing on a warmly lit room
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 따뜻한 조명의 가게 문이 닫히는 장면. 문 앞에 손님이 미소 지으며 돌아보는 모습. 간판에 실제 상호나 로고 없음.
